scene.testo: In Allied custody in 1945, Hermann Göring was asked why Germany invaded the Soviet Union. His answer was not communism. It was not living space. It was a fear of losing oil to Russia.
Who asked him? Where? And why did the man who ran Germany's Four Year Plan talk about oil instead of ideology? The answer begins in a hotel turned prison, and it does not end there.
But oil was only part of what he said. Another part shaped how he said it. The German documents tell a different story from the cell, and the gap between them is the real answer.

The place was Mondorf-les-Bains, a spa town in Luxembourg. The Americans had converted the Palace Hotel into a prison and nicknamed it Ashcan. The date was July 25, 1945. Germany had surrendered eleven weeks earlier.

Göring slept on an army cot. Guards had taken his belt, necktie and razor so he could not take his own life before trial. He arrived overweight and addicted to paracodeine pills, and the Americans weaned him off them.

On May 8, he had surrendered to the Americans, still wearing his uniform. Now he sat in a barred room, waiting to learn what they wanted from him. He was one of the most senior Nazi leaders still alive.

What they wanted was history. Major Kenneth Hechler, an Army historian, was questioning captured German officers for the record. He knew that a wrong question, asked too early, could end the conversation.

So he began carefully. Strategy first. Then America. Then Gibraltar. Hechler did not open with war crimes, because he wanted Göring talking. Only then did he ask about Russia, and the transcript records what he asked.
Was Hitler's fear of Russia military or ideological? Did he fear the spread of communism, or the strength of the Red Army? Göring's answer was short. It would shape his entire defense at trial.
Hitler feared a military attack. That was the one fear he named. Not communism. Not an idea. A Russian army that could one day march west into Germany, and a Soviet state sitting beside the oil.

Then Göring explained where that fear came from. According to him, it began with a visitor in Berlin and a list of demands. The visitor was Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov. The date was November 1940.

Molotov wanted Soviet influence over Finland, Bulgaria, and the Turkish Straits. Göring said it astonished Hitler's circle. Each demand touched something Germany needed: Swedish iron ore through Finland, the Black Sea routes, and, above all, Romania.

Romania was the key. Its Ploesti oilfields were Germany's largest foreign source of oil. German troops had entered the country weeks earlier, in October 1940, officially to train the Romanian army. In fact, they were there to guard the wells.
Göring told Hechler what that meant. If Russia moved toward Romania, it could cut Germany off from oil and grain. And once Finland fell under Russian control, the same would happen to the iron ore.

Oil was Göring's own problem. As head of the Four Year Plan, he was responsible for making Germany less dependent on imports. But Germany had almost no crude oil. Synthetic fuel plants and Romanian wells filled the gap.
A fast war depended on fuel. Panzer divisions, aircraft, and trucks all burned it. The German war machine was built to win quickly, and a long war would drain every barrel the Reich could find.

Yet Soviet oil was already flowing to Germany. Under trade agreements signed in 1939 and 1940, Moscow delivered petroleum, grain, and metals. Deliveries continued right up to the morning of the attack. Hitler was attacking a supplier.

Göring then said Hitler never truly trusted Russia. He saw Soviet rearmament as the great danger of the future. The pact of August 1939 was, in Göring's telling, only a truce, one Hitler never believed in.

Göring said he wanted something else. His plan was to seize Gibraltar, close the Mediterranean, and push toward the Suez Canal. Britain, he argued, might then seek peace. The Luftwaffe would carry the main burden.
What stopped it? Göring gave the same answer again. Fear of Russia. He told Hechler he did not want to attack the Soviet Union, and did not want his air force split between two fronts.

It was a clever defense. Göring portrayed himself as the man who tried to stop the invasion. Historians who studied the interview noted a motive. In 1945, the Americans and the Soviets were already watching each other across Germany.

Göring also said he had warned Hitler against bringing the United States into the war. He called Germany's declaration of war on America a step Germany regretted. These were words chosen for American ears.

scene.testo: Now compare the German records. Göring suggested Molotov's visit was the last straw. But Molotov arrived in Berlin on November 12, 1940, and German planners had been working on an eastern campaign since the summer.

On July 31, 1940, Hitler told his generals that Russia must be destroyed, and he wanted it done in the spring of 1941. Directive 21, Operation Barbarossa, was signed on December 18, 1940, five weeks after Molotov left.

The directive ordered the Wehrmacht to crush Soviet Russia in a rapid campaign, even before the war against England had ended. Nothing in it describes a Soviet attack plan. It describes a conquest, not a defense.
Then there is what Göring left out. His own economic staff planned to exploit the conquered Soviet Union. Its targets were the grain of Ukraine and the oil of the Caucasus. It answered to him.
On May 2, 1941, German officials met to discuss supplies. They wrote that the war could continue only if the army was fed from Russia, and that millions of people there would undoubtedly starve.

Fear alone does not explain this plan. The same men who spoke of Soviet strength were arranging to feed the Wehrmacht on Soviet harvests and fuel its tanks with Soviet oil. Fear and appetite worked together.

In March 1946, Göring took the witness stand at Nuremberg. He claimed he had advised Hitler against the attack. Prosecutor Robert Jackson answered with documents, and with Göring's own role as head of the Four Year Plan.

The tribunal's judgment, delivered on October 1, 1946, found that Göring's only objection to the Soviet war was its timing. Once Hitler decided, Göring followed him without hesitation. He neither refused nor resigned.

The tribunal sentenced him to death by hanging. He had asked to be shot as a soldier. On the night of October 15, 1946, hours before the execution, Göring killed himself with a hidden cyanide capsule.
So was oil the real answer? It was the answer Göring gave, and oil truly mattered. Germany's war economy was fragile. But the fear he described did not cause the invasion. It excused it.

The real motive was conquest. Hitler wanted to destroy the Soviet Union, and take its grain, its oil, and its land. In 1942, his summer offensive aimed straight at the oilfields of Maikop, Grozny, and Baku.

The Germans reached Maikop in August 1942, but Soviet crews had wrecked the wells. Almost no oil flowed. Then Stalingrad turned the campaign, and by early 1943 the Caucasus was lost. The prize never fueled his army.

The oil Göring feared losing was lost anyway. On August 1, 1943, American B-24 bombers flew from Libya to strike Ploesti. In August 1944, Romania switched sides, and Soviet troops entered the oilfields. The very thing he feared had happened.

In 1945, a major asked why Germany invaded Russia, and Göring answered with oil and fear. The records answer differently: conquest, hunger, and a war that ended with Soviet troops standing on the oilfields he feared losing.

descrizione:
In July 1945, in a hotel prison in Luxembourg, an American Army historian asked Hermann Göring why Germany invaded the Soviet Union. His answer centered on fear and oil. This documentary compares Göring's interrogation account with the German records: Directive 21, the Economic Staff East, the Hunger Plan memo of May 1941, and the verdict at Nuremberg.

We follow Molotov's visit to Berlin, the Ploesti oilfields in Romania, the Gibraltar plan Göring claimed to prefer, and the Caucasus offensive of 1942. What did Göring really say, and what do the documents prove about Operation Barbarossa?
